scenario: A demo of an AI ticket router worked on five hand-picked examples. The team wants to launch.
question: What is missing?

options.text: A test set of about 50 real cases, sampled at random with awkward ones added on purpose, scored against written expected answers.
Nothing. Five good results show it works.
More invented examples that cover every category neatly.

why: Demos use friendly examples, are tiny and are judged by feel. A step that is right four times out of five looks perfect in a sample of five and unacceptable at scale.

scenario: The person who built the workflow offers to write the expected answers for the test set since they know it best.
question: Who should write them?

options.text: An experienced operator who knows the work, independent of the builder. Disagreements between experts mean the rule is unclear.
The AI itself, then a person approves.

why: The builder tends to write the answers the workflow would give. Expert disagreement is a finding, because an AI cannot be held to a standard humans cannot agree on.

scenario: Before running the test, the team is asked to set a target. One member says they can decide what counts as passing after seeing the score.
question: When do you set the pass rule?

options.text: Before the test, with a target, a floor for dangerous cases and an action for each outcome.
After seeing results, so the target is realistic.
Never. The numbers will speak for themselves.

why: Once you see a score, it is tempting to adjust the target to fit, and the rule becomes a justification instead of a standard.

scenario: After each failed case, the team tweaks the instructions and re-runs the same 50 cases until they all pass.
question: What went wrong?

options.text: They tuned on the exam. Use part of the set to improve the workflow and hold some cases back as an untouched final check.
Nothing. Passing all 50 shows it is reliable.
They should have tweaked the pass rule instead of the instructions.

why: Tuning on the whole set teaches the step to answer those cases. Splitting roughly 30 for improvement and 20 held back keeps an honest test.

scenario: An AI step flags urgent tickets. Missing a real urgent case is expensive, but a few false alarms are cheap.
question: Which measure do you favor?

options.text: Recall: catching as many truly urgent tickets as possible, accepting more false alarms.
Precision: only flag when it is almost certain.

why: Precision asks how often a flag is right, and recall asks how many real cases were caught. The right balance is a business choice based on the cost of a mistake and belongs in the pass rule.
